1 Samuel 1.summary: Elkanah travels annually with his household to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh. Hannah, distressed by childlessness and provoked by Peninnah, prays silently and promises that if given a son she will devote him to the LORD. Eli initially mistakes her distress for drunkenness but then blesses her. Hannah bears Samuel, waits until he is weaned, and brings him to serve at the sanctuary (1 Samuel 1:1–28). The story introduces Samuel through Hannah’s grief, prayer, and fulfilled commitment, without claiming that every prayer will receive the same answer.
1 Samuel 1.whyItMatters: Pilgrimage sacrifices, shared sacrificial meals, vows, and the stigma attached to infertility frame Hannah’s actions. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. Modern historians differ over details of the emergence and extent of early Israelite kingship; direct external evidence for most named individuals and specific incidents in 1 Samuel is limited.
1 Samuel 1.whereWeAre: According to 1 Samuel 1, Elkanah travels annually with his household to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh. This description is a claim of the biblical narrative, not an assertion that each specific episode is independently documented. Shiloh in the hill country of Ephraim is the principal sanctuary in the story, before Jerusalem became Israel’s royal and temple center. These circumstances clarify the practical and political stakes of the decisions described in 1 Samuel 1.

1 Samuel 2.summary: Hannah praises the LORD for reversing human fortunes: the strong can fall, the weak be raised, and God judges and sustains (1 Samuel 2:1–10). Samuel ministers at Shiloh, while Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas abuse the sacrificial system and treat offerings with contempt 1 Samuel 2:11–17,1 Samuel 2:22–25. Hannah visits Samuel and receives further children (1 Samuel 2:18–21). Eli rebukes his sons, and an unnamed man of God announces judgment on Eli’s house for dishonoring God (1 Samuel 2:27–36). The chapter contrasts faithful worship with religious exploitation.
1 Samuel 2.whyItMatters: Priests received assigned portions of offerings; taking meat improperly and violating worshipers breached sacred responsibilities. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. Modern historians differ over details of the emergence and extent of early Israelite kingship; direct external evidence for most named individuals and specific incidents in 1 Samuel is limited.

1 Samuel 3.summary: As Samuel ministers under Eli, divine revelation is described as uncommon (1 Samuel 3:1). The LORD calls Samuel repeatedly at night; after Eli recognizes what is happening, he instructs the boy how to respond (1 Samuel 3:2–10). God announces judgment on Eli’s household, and Samuel reluctantly reports the message honestly the following morning (1 Samuel 3:11–18). Samuel grows in credibility as a prophet, and word of the LORD continues to reach him at Shiloh (1 Samuel 3:19–21). The account marks Samuel’s emergence as a reliable messenger despite the painful content of his first recorded revelation.

1 Samuel 4.summary: Israel loses a battle against the Philistines and brings the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, hoping its presence will ensure victory (1 Samuel 4:1–5). The Philistines fight again, defeat Israel, capture the ark, and kill Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas (1 Samuel 4:6–11). News of the defeat and ark’s capture reaches Eli, who falls and dies (1 Samuel 4:12–18). Phinehas’s wife gives birth as she dies and names the child Ichabod, linking the disaster with departed glory (1 Samuel 4:19–22). The chapter warns against treating a sacred object as a guarantee of success.

Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 5.summary: The Philistines place the captured ark in Dagon’s temple at Ashdod. Their deity’s statue falls before it, and on the second morning its head and hands are broken (1 Samuel 5:1–5). Severe affliction strikes Ashdod and later Gath and Ekron as the ark is moved among Philistine cities (1 Samuel 5:6–12). The Philistines come to fear keeping it. The narrative presents the LORD as sovereign even when Israel has lost and the ark is outside Israelite control. The exact medical nature of the affliction is not identified with certainty.

1 Samuel 6.summary: After seven months the Philistines consult priests and diviners about returning the ark (1 Samuel 6:1–9). They send it on a new cart drawn by two cows with offerings of gold models representing their afflictions and rodents (1 Samuel 6:10–12). The cows go to Beth-shemesh, where people rejoice and offer sacrifices (1 Samuel 6:13–18). Yet some Beth-shemesh residents are struck down in connection with their treatment of the ark, and the community asks the people of Kiriath-jearim to take it away (1 Samuel 6:19–21). Manuscripts and translations differ about the exact death toll in verse 19.

Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 7.summary: The ark is taken to Kiriath-jearim, where Eleazar is appointed to guard it; many years pass (1 Samuel 7:1–2). Samuel calls Israel to put away foreign gods and return to the LORD, and the people gather at Mizpah for confession and prayer (1 Samuel 7:3–6). As Philistines approach, Samuel offers sacrifice and cries to God; Israel wins the encounter and Samuel erects a memorial stone named Ebenezer (1 Samuel 7:7–12). The narrator describes a period of relief from Philistine pressure and Samuel’s continuing circuit as judge (1 Samuel 7:13–17).

1 Samuel 8.summary: Samuel becomes old, and his sons Joel and Abijah pervert justice in Beersheba (1 Samuel 8:1–3). Israel’s elders ask for a king to judge them like surrounding nations (1 Samuel 8:4–5). God tells Samuel to heed them but explain how a king may conscript sons, employ daughters, seize resources, and tax the people (1 Samuel 8:6–18). The elders insist that a king should judge and lead them in battle (1 Samuel 8:19–22). The chapter explores the tension between understandable concerns about corrupt leadership and the danger of centralized power.
1 Samuel 8.whyItMatters: Royal requisitions, forced labor, household servants, and taxation were recognizable features of ancient Near Eastern kingship. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 9.summary: Saul, a Benjaminite son of Kish, searches for his father’s missing donkeys with a servant (1 Samuel 9:1–5). The servant suggests consulting a man of God; they travel to a town where Samuel is expected (1 Samuel 9:6–14). The LORD has informed Samuel that a Benjaminite will arrive and is to be designated as leader over Israel (1 Samuel 9:15–17). Samuel meets Saul, assures him the donkeys are found, seats him at a sacrificial meal, and prepares to disclose God’s message (1 Samuel 9:18–27). An ordinary errand becomes the setting for Saul’s public life.

Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 10.summary: Samuel privately anoints Saul as ruler and gives three signs that are fulfilled on Saul’s journey (1 Samuel 10:1–13). Samuel assembles Israel at Mizpah and reminds them of the LORD’s past deliverance before selecting Saul publicly by lot (1 Samuel 10:17–24). Saul is found hiding among supplies, then presented to the people; some celebrate him while others question his ability (1 Samuel 10:23–27). The chapter brings together private designation, confirming signs, and public recognition while preserving the narrator’s unease about Israel’s demand for a king.

1 Samuel 11.summary: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and proposes a humiliating condition of surrender (1 Samuel 11:1–2). The besieged send messengers, and Saul, hearing the news, rallies Israelites to confront the threat (1 Samuel 11:3–8). Saul’s forces attack the Ammonites and deliver Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11:9–11). He refuses to execute those who had opposed him, and Samuel calls the people to Gilgal, where Saul’s kingship is reaffirmed with sacrifices and celebration (1 Samuel 11:12–15). The episode shows Saul’s early effectiveness and a moment of national solidarity.

1 Samuel 12.summary: Samuel challenges the people to name any way he has defrauded or exploited them; they affirm his integrity (1 Samuel 12:1–5). He reviews the LORD’s acts of deliverance and Israel’s repeated failures to remember them (1 Samuel 12:6–12). Although the monarchy is now established, he urges both king and people to fear and obey the LORD (1 Samuel 12:13–15). Samuel calls for thunder and rain during wheat harvest as a sign; the people acknowledge wrongdoing, and he promises to continue praying for them and teaching the good way (1 Samuel 12:16–25).

1 Samuel 13.summary: A new phase of conflict with the Philistines begins after Jonathan attacks a Philistine post (1 Samuel 13:1–5). The Philistine response frightens Israelite forces, who scatter or hide (1 Samuel 13:5–7). Saul waits for Samuel at Gilgal but offers the burnt offering himself before Samuel arrives (1 Samuel 13:8–10). Samuel rebukes him for disobeying divine instruction and announces that Saul’s dynasty will not endure (1 Samuel 13:11–14). The chapter ends by stressing Israel’s military disadvantage, including restricted access to ironworking and weapons (1 Samuel 13:15–23). The Hebrew text of 13:1 has numerical problems, so Saul’s age and regnal total there are uncertain.
1 Samuel 13.whyItMatters: Burnt offerings belonged to Israel’s worship, while smithing and metal weapons figured in regional military inequality. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 14.summary: Jonathan and his armor-bearer climb toward a Philistine position, trusting that the LORD is able to save with few or many (1 Samuel 14:1–15). Panic spreads among the Philistines, and Saul joins the pursuit (1 Samuel 14:16–23). Saul has bound the troops with a fasting oath; Jonathan, unaware, eats honey and later challenges the decision’s effect on the exhausted men (1 Samuel 14:24–30). The troops sin by eating meat with blood, and Saul attempts to deal with the violation (1 Samuel 14:31–35). When a lot identifies Jonathan as the oath-breaker, the people prevent his execution (1 Samuel 14:36–46). The chapter closes with Saul’s wars and household (1 Samuel 14:47–52).
1 Samuel 14.whyItMatters: Oaths carried religious weight; the ban on eating blood explains the troops’ wrongdoing (14:32–34). Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 15.summary: Samuel instructs Saul to carry out judgment against Amalek, including a command of total destruction in the narrative (1 Samuel 15:1–3). Saul defeats Amalek but spares King Agag and keeps prized livestock (1 Samuel 15:4–9). Samuel confronts him, and Saul attempts to defend his actions by invoking sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:10–21). Samuel insists that obedience matters more than offerings (1 Samuel 15:22–23). Saul acknowledges sin, Samuel announces rejection of Saul’s kingship, Agag is killed, and Samuel separates from Saul (1 Samuel 15:24–35). The chapter’s violent command belongs to an ancient war narrative and raises substantial modern ethical questions; it should not be used to justify present-day violence.
1 Samuel 15.whyItMatters: The Hebrew concept of devotion to destruction (herem) appears in ancient warfare texts; description of the command is not a modern ethical endorsement. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 16.summary: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a son of Jesse as Saul’s successor (1 Samuel 16:1–5). Samuel sees Jesse’s older sons, but none is chosen; the LORD tells him that divine evaluation is not limited to outward appearance (1 Samuel 16:6–10). David, tending sheep, is brought in and anointed, and the Spirit comes upon him (1 Samuel 16:11–13). Meanwhile Saul is afflicted by a troubling spirit in the narrative, and David is brought to play the lyre and serve in Saul’s court (1 Samuel 16:14–23). David’s rise begins before he receives political power.
1 Samuel 16.whyItMatters: Anointing with oil marks selection; shepherding and lyre-playing were practical activities in the ancient setting. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 17.summary: Philistine and Israelite forces face each other in the Valley of Elah, where Goliath challenges Israel (1 Samuel 17:1–11). David arrives bringing supplies to his brothers and questions the fear that grips the camp (1 Samuel 17:12–30). Saul initially doubts David’s readiness, but David recalls protecting sheep from predators and attributes rescue to the LORD (1 Samuel 17:31–37). Refusing Saul’s armor, David confronts Goliath with a sling and stone, kills him, and the Philistines flee (1 Samuel 17:38–54). Saul asks about David’s family (1 Samuel 17:55–58). Ancient witnesses differ in the length and details of this chapter, and the stated height of Goliath varies among textual traditions.

Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 18.summary: Jonathan forms a close covenant relationship with David and gives him clothing and weapons as tokens of commitment (1 Samuel 18:1–4). David succeeds in military service and becomes widely praised, while Saul grows angry and fearful (1 Samuel 18:5–16). Saul offers Merab, then Michal, in marriage under circumstances designed to expose David to danger; David marries Michal after fulfilling Saul’s demanded bride-price (1 Samuel 18:17–29). Saul increasingly views David as an enemy (1 Samuel 18:29–30). The narrator contrasts Jonathan’s loyalty with Saul’s escalating hostility.

Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 19.summary: Saul orders David’s death, but Jonathan warns David and persuades his father to spare him temporarily (1 Samuel 19:1–7). When conflict returns, Saul attacks David, and David escapes (1 Samuel 19:8–10). Michal helps David flee through a window and delays the pursuers using a household image in his bed (1 Samuel 19:11–17). David reaches Samuel at Ramah, where successive groups sent to seize him, and finally Saul himself, prophesy in an episode presented as frustrating the arrest (1 Samuel 19:18–24). The chapter underscores David’s vulnerability even within the royal family.

Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 20.summary: David tells Jonathan he fears Saul intends to kill him, despite Jonathan’s initial disbelief (1 Samuel 20:1–11). The friends renew their covenant, including concern for Jonathan’s descendants (1 Samuel 20:12–23). Jonathan tests Saul’s intentions during a new-moon meal and discovers his father’s hostility toward David and toward Jonathan’s loyalty (1 Samuel 20:24–34). Jonathan signals the danger by shooting arrows near a boy, then meets David for a tearful farewell and reaffirmation of their oath (1 Samuel 20:35–42). The chapter shows costly loyalty amid the rupture of family and political bonds.

1 Samuel 21.summary: David arrives at Nob and receives consecrated bread from Ahimelech the priest after giving an explanation of his mission (1 Samuel 21:1–6). He also obtains Goliath’s sword, which had been kept there (1 Samuel 21:7–9). Doeg the Edomite, a servant of Saul, is present (1 Samuel 21:7). David then flees to Achish, king of Gath; fearful when recognized, he alters his behavior to appear insane, and Achish dismisses him (1 Samuel 21:10–15). The narrative stresses the uncertainty and precarious improvisation of David’s flight, while raising questions about his misleading speech at Nob.

1 Samuel 22.summary: David gathers family members and distressed or indebted followers at the cave of Adullam, then seeks shelter for his parents in Moab (1 Samuel 22:1–5). Meanwhile Saul accuses his servants and Jonathan of conspiring against him (1 Samuel 22:6–8). Doeg reports Ahimelech’s assistance to David; Saul summons the priests of Nob and orders their execution despite Ahimelech’s defense (1 Samuel 22:9–18). Doeg kills the priests, and Nob’s population is slaughtered (1 Samuel 22:18–19). Abiathar escapes to David, who accepts responsibility for the danger that befell his family (1 Samuel 22:20–23).

1 Samuel 23.summary: David learns that Philistines are raiding Keilah and consults the LORD before attacking and rescuing the city (1 Samuel 23:1–5). Saul prepares to trap him there, but David consults the LORD again through Abiathar and leaves before being handed over (1 Samuel 23:6–13). Jonathan visits David and strengthens him with reassurance (1 Samuel 23:14–18). The Ziphites reveal David’s location, and Saul pursues him in the wilderness until news of a Philistine raid forces Saul to withdraw (1 Samuel 23:19–29). The chapter shows both David’s help to others and his continuing instability.

1 Samuel 24.summary: Saul pursues David into the wilderness of En-gedi and enters a cave where David’s men are hiding (1 Samuel 24:1–3). David cuts off a corner of Saul’s robe but regrets even that gesture and refuses to kill the LORD’s anointed king (1 Samuel 24:4–7). After Saul departs, David calls out, shows the cloth as proof he spared Saul, and appeals for judgment from the LORD (1 Samuel 24:8–15). Saul acknowledges David’s restraint, foresees his rise, and asks for protection of his descendants (1 Samuel 24:16–22). The chapter contrasts opportunity for revenge with chosen restraint.

1 Samuel 25.summary: Samuel dies and is mourned (1 Samuel 25:1). David’s men ask the wealthy Nabal for provisions after having been near his shepherds, but Nabal contemptuously refuses (1 Samuel 25:2–13). Abigail, Nabal’s wife, gathers food and intervenes before David can attack his household, urging him not to incur bloodguilt and appealing to his future (1 Samuel 25:14–31). David praises her discretion and withdraws (1 Samuel 25:32–35). Nabal later dies, Abigail marries David, and the chapter also reports David’s marriage to Ahinoam and Saul’s giving Michal to another man (1 Samuel 25:36–44).
1 Samuel 25.whyItMatters: Sheep shearing could involve feasting and distribution; hospitality expectations explain the request but do not justify violent retaliation. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 26.summary: Ziphites alert Saul to David’s position near Hachilah, and Saul camps nearby (1 Samuel 26:1–5). David and Abishai enter Saul’s camp by night and find him asleep; Abishai offers to kill him, but David refuses and takes only Saul’s spear and water jar (1 Samuel 26:6–12). From a distance David rebukes Abner for failing to guard the king, then challenges Saul to explain the pursuit (1 Samuel 26:13–20). Saul acknowledges wrongdoing, and the two part ways after David returns the spear (1 Samuel 26:21–25). This is a distinct narrated episode that echoes chapter 24.

1 Samuel 27.summary: David concludes Saul will eventually capture him and moves with six hundred men and their households to Achish of Gath (1 Samuel 27:1–4). Achish grants him Ziklag as a base (1 Samuel 27:5–7). David raids groups in the southern region, reports misleading targets to Achish, and leaves no survivors to contradict him (1 Samuel 27:8–12). Achish comes to trust David, believing he has made himself offensive to Israel. The chapter describes morally troubling violence and deception without issuing a blanket endorsement of David’s conduct.

1 Samuel 28.summary: As the Philistines gather, Saul sees their camp and is afraid; he receives no answer through the channels of inquiry the account lists (1 Samuel 28:1–6). Despite having expelled mediums, he seeks one at En-dor in disguise and asks her to summon Samuel (1 Samuel 28:7–11). The narrative describes an appearance identified as Samuel, who announces that the kingdom has been torn from Saul and predicts defeat and death (1 Samuel 28:12–19). Saul collapses, and the woman and his servants persuade him to eat before departing (1 Samuel 28:20–25). Interpretations differ on the mechanics of the apparition; the narrative’s stated identification should be distinguished from later explanations.
1 Samuel 28.whyItMatters: Necromancy was prohibited in Israelite law (see Leviticus 19:31); the account narrates the episode but does not recommend the practice. Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text. 1 Samuel 29.summary: As the Philistines assemble at Aphek and the Israelites near Jezreel, David and his men march with Achish (1 Samuel 29:1–2). Other Philistine commanders object to David’s participation, fearing he could change sides in battle (1 Samuel 29:3–5). Although Achish defends David’s conduct, he sends him back to Philistine territory to avoid provoking the commanders (1 Samuel 29:6–11). David’s words suggest a willingness to fight, but the narrative does not disclose with certainty what he intended to do had he been allowed to participate.

1 Samuel 30.summary: David and his men return to Ziklag to find it burned and their families taken captive by Amalekite raiders (1 Samuel 30:1–6). Under pressure from his distressed followers, David finds strength in the LORD, seeks guidance through Abiathar, and sets out in pursuit (1 Samuel 30:6–10). An abandoned Egyptian servant provides information, and David’s force defeats the raiders and recovers the captives and goods (1 Samuel 30:11–20). David requires those who stayed with supplies to share the recovered goods with those who fought, and sends gifts to Judahite towns (1 Samuel 30:21–31).

1 Samuel 31.summary: The Philistines rout the Israelites on Mount Gilboa and kill Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua (1 Samuel 31:1–2). Saul is severely wounded by archers and, fearing abuse by the enemy, falls on his own sword after his armor-bearer refuses to kill him (1 Samuel 31:3–6). Israelites abandon nearby towns, and the Philistines display the bodies of Saul and his sons at Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:7–10). Men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve the bodies, burn them, bury their bones, and fast seven days (1 Samuel 31:11–13). The book ends with royal defeat, grief, and an act of remembered loyalty.

Reading these details in their setting helps explain the chapter without assuming every action narrated is approved by the text.
